# Trace Commons — Agent Traces

**Trace Commons** is one open, public dataset of coding-agent sessions — the
back-and-forth between a developer and an AI coding agent, including prompts,
model responses, tool calls, and command output — contributed voluntarily as an
open resource for studying, evaluating, and building on how these agents
actually work.

Every trace here was donated **only from a public, open-source repository**, was
**anonymized on the contributor's own machine before upload**, and was
**reviewed by the contributor** before it was submitted as a pull request.

## What's in it

Every session is preserved as its agent's **raw, unmodified session file** (only
anonymized, never reshaped), organized by which agent (harness) produced it:

```
sessions/claude_code/<file>.jsonl
sessions/codex/<file>.jsonl
sessions/pi/<file>.jsonl
sessions/cursor/<file>.jsonl
sessions/opencode/<file>.json
```

The **dataset table you see in the viewer** is built from these raw files,
decoded one row per session (`harness`, `session_id`, `prompt`, `messages`,
`tools`, `trace`, `metadata`, …) and served as Parquet under `data/` for
reliable loading. The raw `sessions/` files remain the source of truth — download
them directly to work with the original agent-native format.

## How traces are collected

Traces are donated with the **[`donate-trace`](https://github.com/trace-commons-ai/donate-trace)**
skill, installable into a coding agent. The skill:

1. Confirms the session's project is a public, open-source repository — and
   refuses otherwise.
2. Locates the current session from the agent's own local logs.
3. Runs a deterministic scrubber (`scrub.py`) **locally** to strip the
   highest-confidence leaks (see below).
4. Asks the contributor to review what was removed, and shows the cleaned trace.
5. Only after explicit confirmation, opens a **pull request** — either under the
   contributor's own Hugging Face account (attributed) or anonymously through the
   Trace Commons ingestion server, which re-runs the same scrubber as a backstop.

Nothing is pushed directly; a maintainer reviews every pull request before it
becomes part of the dataset.

## Anonymization — and its limits

Anonymization happens in two passes:

- **Deterministic pass (`scrub.py`).** Removes things with crisp signatures:
  home-directory paths and the username inside them, common secret formats (AWS,
  GitHub/GitLab, Slack, Google/GCP, OpenAI/Anthropic, Stripe, Twilio, SendGrid,
  npm/PyPI tokens, Azure storage keys, JWTs, PEM private-key blocks, `KEY=value`
  env-var secrets, bearer tokens, DB connection strings, webhook URLs), and email
  addresses.
- **Scanner backstop (`TruffleHog`).** Because a hand-written pattern list can
  never be complete, the ingestion server additionally runs
  [TruffleHog](https://github.com/trufflesecurity/trufflehog) — hundreds of
  maintained secret detectors — over every donation (the regex pass above is the
  fast, high-confidence hard block; TruffleHog adds breadth). It runs without
  verification, so candidate secrets are never sent to any third party — which
  also means it can false-positive on high-entropy strings, so its findings
  **flag a donation for maintainer review** rather than auto-rejecting it. Every
  donation is reviewed by a maintainer before it is merged regardless.

- **Review pass (human + agent judgment).** Catches what a regex cannot:
  personal names, company or client names, internal hostnames, codenames, ticket
  IDs in free-text prose.

> **Anonymization is best-effort and imperfect.** The deterministic pass only
> catches patterns it knows about; the review pass depends on human judgment and
> can miss things. **Do not assume this data is free of personal information.**
> A name, an internal URL, a company reference, or a novel secret format can slip
> through. Treat these traces as public material that has been carefully but
> imperfectly cleaned — not as guaranteed-anonymous data.

If you find sensitive information in a trace, please use the takedown path below.

## License

The **Trace Commons compilation** — the collection, its structure, and its
metadata — is released under **[CC-BY-4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)**.
You may use, share, and build on it (including for training) with attribution to
Trace Commons.

Individual traces may contain source code, file contents, command output, and
other material that carries its own original licensing. Traces are accepted on
the basis of the **contributor's certification**: by donating, a contributor
certifies that the session is not private or confidential and that they have the
right to publish it publicly under this license. That certification — not
maintainer vetting — is what traces rest on; we do not and cannot verify the
provenance or license of everything inside every trace. Maintainers review for
quality and obvious secret/PII leakage, not to re-confirm the contributor's
right to share.

**If you reuse this data, you are responsible for checking that your use complies
with the licenses of any code or content contained in the traces.** Likewise,
contributors are responsible for only donating sessions they have the right to
share — sessions from public, open-source work that contain no employer, client,
or otherwise confidential material — and for complying with the terms of the
coding-agent provider they used (for example Anthropic's or OpenAI's terms). If
something shouldn't be here, use the takedown path below.

## Privacy & personal data

These traces can contain **personal data** — names, email addresses, identifiers,

# Cline Incident Traces

Real coding-agent sessions in which the agent did something unsafe, adversarial, or concerning, contributed by the people who were sitting in front of it. Each session is a redacted transcript, an [ATIF](https://github.com/laude-institute/harbor) trajectory, a structured write-up by the contributor, and, when licensing allows, a snapshot of the repository at the start of the session so the situation can be reproduced.

The dataset exists so that the people training and evaluating models have access to real examples of agents going wrong on real repositories, not only curated benchmarks. Contributions come through the [`/upload-hf`](https://github.com/cline/upload-hf) Cline plugin as pull requests to this repository, and every one is reviewed before merge.

## What is in a session

```
sessions/<session_hash>/
  SUBMISSION.md      contributor's write-up: categories, severity, what happened, where to look
  messages.json      redacted native transcript (Cline messages contract v1)
  trajectory.json    ATIF-v1.7 trajectory with outcome signals
  meta.json          model, provider, repository URL and license, outcome, redaction summary
  findings.json      redaction counts by detector (never values)
  solution.patch     the agent's changes as a unified diff, when there were any
  repo.tar.gz        repository at session start, only for permissive public repositories
manifest.jsonl       one line per session for filtering by category, severity, model, repository
```

`SUBMISSION.md` is the entry point. Its frontmatter carries the labels (see [TAXONOMY.md](TAXONOMY.md)) and `key_messages`, the message indices where the incident happens. Its body is the contributor's account in five fixed sections: what they asked for, what the agent did, what they expected, why they are contributing, and notes for reviewers.

`session_hash` is a truncated SHA-256 of the Cline session id. Working paths, process ids, and raw session ids are never included.

## Using the data

Filter `manifest.jsonl` first. Every line has `categories`, `severity`, `adversarial`, `provider`, `model`, `repository_license`, and `snapshot`, so you can select, for example, high-severity `prompt-injection` incidents from a single model family with a snapshot available.

Traces record which model produced each step. Several providers restrict the use of their outputs for training other models. Check the provider's terms before training on a session; the `provider` and `model` fields exist so you can build a compliant subset.

## How sessions were redacted

Each session went through a deterministic pass (known secrets, credential patterns, home paths, e-mail addresses, contributor-supplied literals and deny-list regexes), a full read-through by the contributor's own agent with a written verdict, and the contributor's explicit confirmation. Sessions were then scanned again during review. If you find something that should not be here, see below.

## Contributing

Install the plugin and run `/upload-hf` in the session you want to report. The agent walks you through redaction review, the write-up, and the pull request. Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) first, in particular the section on what not to submit.

## Removal

Open a discussion titled `Removal request: <session_hash>`. We remove the session, rebuild the manifest, and request a history purge from Hugging Face when the request involves sensitive data.

## License

Transcripts, trajectories, and write-ups are licensed under CC-BY-4.0 by their contributors. Source code inside `repo.tar.gz` and `solution.patch` keeps the license of its repository, recorded in `meta.json` as `repository_license`.

# Claude Cowork agent trace: AI stack regulation tweet + diagram

A single-session agent trace from Claude (Cowork mode), in raw Claude Code JSONL session format, natively supported by the [Hugging Face agent trace viewer](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/agent-traces).

## What happens in this session

The session covers an iterative content creation workflow:

1. Drafting a long tweet arguing that model weights, APIs, and apps sit at different layers of the AI stack and should be regulated differently
2. Generating a 16:9 diagram of the three layers (HTML rendered to PNG via headless Chromium, with a colorblind-safe validated palette)
3. Several rounds of iteration: adding a car-industry analogy (steel / parts suppliers / cars), simplifying the graph, reverting, keeping tweet and graph in sync
4. Fact-checking the analogy (whether steel is regulated for car safety) with web search
5. Packaging and sharing this very trace as a dataset

## Notes

- Agent: Claude (Cowork), Claude Code JSONL session format
- Date: 2026-08-05
- The trace includes tool calls (file edits, shell, screenshots, web search) and base64-embedded screenshots of the rendered diagram

# Claude World Cup 2026 Wallchart — Agent Traces

Anonymized Claude Code session traces from the run that predicted all of the World Cup 2026 matches and built and deployed the **[victor/claude-worldcup-2026-wallchart](https://huggingface.co/spaces/victor/claude-worldcup-2026-wallchart)** Space.

The single prompt that kicked it off:

> *ultracode to pronostic every matches of the world cup 2026 until you have a winner once done build a visualization and push it in a static space*

## How it was built

- **Orchestrator (main loop):** Fable (`claude-fable-5`)
- **Worker subagents:** Sonnet 4.6 (`claude-sonnet-4-6`), fanned out via a Claude Code Workflow

Fable ran the top-level session, scouted the real tournament field, and spun up a multi-agent workflow whose Sonnet worker agents predicted the matches in parallel. Fable then assembled the visualization and pushed it to a static Space. You can confirm the models directly from the traces (`message.model` on each record).

## Structure

```
data/
  session.jsonl                       # main Fable orchestrator session
  subagents/                          # spawned agents
    agent-*.jsonl
    workflows/wf_*/agent-*.jsonl      # Sonnet worker agents from the workflow
  workflow/worldcup-2026-pronostic.js # the workflow script that drove the fan-out
```

Each `.jsonl` line is one record (`user` or `assistant`) with the original `message` payload and minimal threading metadata (`uuid`, `parentUuid`, `timestamp`).

## Anonymization

These traces were scrubbed before release. Specifically:

- **Removed entirely:** all harness-injected context (the available-skills catalog, MCP server lists and tool schemas), file-history snapshots, hook/system bookkeeping, and per-record environment metadata (`cwd`, `gitBranch`, `version`, session/request IDs).
- **Blanked:** outputs of browser (MCP), `ToolSearch`, and `Skill` calls (these reflected live local/private state such as screenshots and open browser tabs), and all embedded images.
- **Neutralized in text:** local filesystem paths, MCP/skill identifiers, and any IPs/tokens/emails (none of the latter were present).
- **Kept:** the public author handle `victor` and the public Space slug, since the Space is already public.

The `victor` handle is intentionally retained; everything else identifying was removed.

# MISC Unification of Public Claude Code Traces

A unified dataset of **32,133 deduplicated Claude API conversation traces** focused on software engineering and code generation tasks. This dataset merges and normalizes traces from 10 different source datasets into a single, consistent format.

## Dataset Description

This dataset contains real Claude API interaction traces capturing software engineering workflows including:
- Code generation and modification
- Bug fixing and debugging
- Repository exploration
- Git operations
- Tool use (Bash, file operations, etc.)

### Sources

The dataset was created by merging and deduplicating the following Hugging Face datasets:

| Source | Original Rows | Description |
|--------|---------------|-------------|
| `archit11/complete-conversations-dataset` | 59,990 | Claude Code conversation traces |
| `archit11/claude_traces_hs` | 784 | Hyperswitch repository traces with git diffs |
| `archit11/claude_traces_hs2` | 784 | Hyperswitch traces with Claude logs |
| `archit11/claude-code-traces` | 25 | Claude Code API traces |
| `archit11/out_dataset` | 59 | Claude agent outputs |
| `robin0307/claude-code-mend` | 100 | Claude Code mending traces |

Additional normalized views from prior merge efforts were also included. After deduplication (by content hash of user prompt + assistant response), **32,133 unique conversations** remain.

## Dataset Schema

| Column | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `id` | string | Unique identifier (UUID) |
| `source_table` | string | Original source table name |
| `source_repo` | string | Original HuggingFace repo |
| `messages_json` | string | Full conversation as JSON array of `{role, content}` |
| `system_prompt` | string | System prompt if available |
| `user_prompt` | string | Extracted user message content |
| `assistant_response` | string | Extracted assistant response content |
| `model` | string | Claude model used (e.g., `claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929`) |
| `timestamp` | string | ISO timestamp of the interaction |
| `request_id` | string | API request ID if available |
| `tools_json` | string | Tool definitions as JSON if available |
| `gitdiff` | string | Git diff context if available |
| `claude_log` | string | Claude execution logs if available |
| `chatml` | string | Original ChatML format if applicable |
| `has_empty_response` | bool | True if assistant response is empty/missing |
| `content_hash` | string | MD5 hash of (user_prompt + assistant_response) for deduplication |

## Model Distribution

| Model | Count |
|-------|-------|
| claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 | 20,414 |
| claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 | 10,900 |
| claude-3-5-haiku-20241022 | 23 |
| (not recorded) | 796 |

## Usage

```python
from datasets import load_dataset

# Load the dataset
dataset = load_dataset("nlile/claude-code-traces-unified")

# Filter to only rows with responses
with_responses = dataset.filter(lambda x: not x["has_empty_response"])

# Access a conversation
example = dataset["train"][0]
print(f"User: {example['user_prompt'][:200]}...")
print(f"Assistant: {example['assistant_response'][:200]}...")
```

### Working with messages_json

```python
import json

example = dataset["train"][0]
if example["messages_json"]:
    messages = json.loads(example["messages_json"])
    for msg in messages:
        print(f"{msg['role']}: {msg['content'][:100]}...")
```

## Data Quality Notes

- **6,685 rows** (~20%) have empty assistant responses - these are incomplete conversations where only the user turn was recorded
- All rows have been deduplicated by content hash
- Original raw data is preserved in source columns for traceability
- Some conversations contain tool use (Bash commands, file operations) embedded in the assistant responses

# ClaudeCode in Anthropic Tools API format

## About AgentIR Collection

This dataset is part of the **[AgentIR Collection](https://huggingface.co/WhitzardAgent)**.
AgentIR is an open-source compiler infrastructure for agentic trajectories (like LLVM/MLIR, but for agent traces).
Using AgentIR, you can convert any source trajectory format into multiple target formats.

- Project: https://github.com/ravenSanstete/agentir
- DSL: Define custom formats with `*.agentir.yaml` files
- CLI: `agentir dsl convert` for one-command format conversion

## Dataset Description

- **Source dataset:** [nlile/misc-merged-claude-code-traces-v1](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nlile/misc-merged-claude-code-traces-v1)
- **Target format:** Anthropic Tools API format
- **Rows:** 32,133
- **License:** apache-2.0



## Format Details

Messages with typed content blocks (`text`, `tool_use`, `tool_result`). Tool results appear as `user` role messages per the Anthropic API convention.

### Record Structure

Each record contains a `messages` field with the converted trajectory data.

```json
{
  "messages": [
    {"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Fix the bug"}]},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "..."}, {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_1", "name": "terminal", "input": {...}}]},
    {"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_1", "content": [...]}]}
  ],
  "tools": [...]
}
```

## Conversion

This dataset was generated using AgentIR v0.1.0:

```bash
# Step 1: Convert source to AgentIR Canonical
agentir dsl convert dsl/formats/claude_code.agentir.yaml data.jsonl -o canonical.air.jsonl

# Step 2: Lower to target format
agentir-llc --input canonical.air.jsonl --target anthropic-tools --output output.jsonl
```

### Pass Pipeline

```
parse-claude-log, canonicalize-tools, pair-tool-results, extract-patches, normalize-outcome, verify
```

## Conversion Statistics

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Source records | 32,133 |
| Source events | 6,760 (estimated) |
| Success rate | 100% (0 failures) |
| Throughput | 1,811 records/sec (AgentTrove full benchmark) |

## Usage

```python
from datasets import load_dataset

ds = load_dataset("WhitzardAgent/ClaudeCode-Anthropic", split="train")
print(ds[0])
```

### Re-convert to Other Formats

Since this is an AgentIR-formatted dataset, you can re-convert it to any other target:

```bash
# Convert to OpenAI format
agentir-llc --input canonical.air.jsonl --target openai-tools --output openai.jsonl

# Convert to Anthropic format
agentir-llc --input canonical.air.jsonl --target anthropic-tools --output anthropic.jsonl

# Convert to Hermes XML
agentir-llc --input canonical.air.jsonl --target hermes-xml --output hermes.jsonl --include-reasoning
```

## Quality Verification

All conversions passed automated verification:
1. Source dataset field completeness check
2. Role mapping correctness verification (user/assistant/tool/system)
3. Event type inference accuracy verification
4. Zero record errors (100% success rate)
5. Schema compliance validated with `agentir verify`

# Codex SWE-Bench Pro — OTel Traces

OpenTelemetry-formatted LLM traces derived from
[Inferact/codex_swebenchpro_traces](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Inferact/codex_swebenchpro_traces),
a collection of agentic Codex runs on the
[SWE-bench Pro](https://www.swebench.com/) software-engineering benchmark.

## Overview

Each row in the source dataset is a full multi-turn agent conversation where a
Codex agent resolves a real GitHub issue. This dataset re-represents those
conversations as **OpenTelemetry GenAI spans**, one span per LLM call, using
cumulative message history so that each span captures exactly what the model
received and produced at that step.

**Note on assistant message content:** The source dataset redacts all model
outputs — every assistant message is replaced with lorem ipsum placeholder
text. User-side messages (tool outputs, shell command results, file contents)
are real. This dataset is therefore useful for studying LLM input structure
and context growth patterns, but not model output behavior.

**Note on model identity:** The source dataset does not expose a model
identifier. `gen_ai.request.model` and `gen_ai.response.model` are set to
`"unknown"`.

## License

Released under [CC-BY-NC-4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/).

## Conversion Logic

For a conversation with turns `[user₁, assistant₁, user₂, assistant₂, …]`:

| Span | `gen_ai.input.messages` | `gen_ai.output.messages` |
|------|------------------------|--------------------------|
| 1 | `[user₁]` | `[assistant₁]` |
| 2 | `[user₁, assistant₁, user₂]` | `[assistant₂]` |
| 3 | `[user₁, assistant₁, user₂, assistant₂, user₃]` | `[assistant₃]` |

Timestamps are synthetic: spans within a trace are spaced with random
1–10 second delays (no real wall-clock timing data was available in the source).

## Dataset Statistics

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| Total traces | 610 |
| Total spans | 20,230 |
| Mean spans / trace | 33.2 |
| Median spans / trace | 30 |
| Min / max spans / trace | 6 / 100 |

## Dataset Structure

Each file is a single-line JSONL object (one trace per line):

```json
{
  "trace_id": "<32-char hex>",
  "span_count": 11,
  "collected_at": "<ISO timestamp>",
  "spans": [...]
}
```

Each span:

```json
{
  "trace_id": "...",
  "span_id": "...",
  "parent_span_id": null,
  "name": "chat unknown",
  "kind": "SPAN_KIND_CLIENT",
  "start_time": "2026-05-24T07:52:24.216485",
  "end_time": "2026-05-24T07:52:24.216485",
  "attributes": {
    "gen_ai.operation.name": "chat",
    "gen_ai.request.model": "unknown",
    "gen_ai.response.model": "unknown",
    "gen_ai.input.messages": "<JSON-encoded message array>",
    "gen_ai.output.messages": "<JSON-encoded message array>",
    "gen_ai.tool.definitions": "[]"
  },
  "resource_attributes": {
    "telemetry.sdk.language": "python",
    "telemetry.sdk.name": "codex",
    "telemetry.sdk.version": "1.0.0",
    "service.name": "codex",
    "service.version": "1.0.0"
  },
  "status": { "code": 1, "message": "" }
}
```

Note: `gen_ai.input.messages` and `gen_ai.output.messages` are **JSON-encoded strings**
(not parsed arrays). Each message follows the OTel GenAI format:

```json
{ "role": "user" | "assistant", "parts": [{ "type": "text", "content": "..." }] }
```

## Usage

```python
import json
from datasets import load_dataset

ds = load_dataset("json", data_files="*.jsonl", split="train")

# Each row is one trace
trace = ds[0]
print(f"{trace['span_count']} spans in this trace")

# Iterate spans
for span in trace["spans"]:
    attrs = span["attributes"]
    input_msgs = json.loads(attrs["gen_ai.input.messages"])
    output_msgs = json.loads(attrs["gen_ai.output.messages"])
    print(f"span {span['span_id']} — {len(input_msgs)} input messages")
    for msg in output_msgs:
        for part in msg.get("parts", []):
            print(f"  [{msg['role']}] {part['content'][:100]}")
```

- **Task:** SWE-bench Pro — resolving GitHub issues across 11 open-source Python repositories
- **Agent:** Codex (OpenAI)
- **Original size:** 610 successful trials out of 731 total (~54% pass rate)

# ClaudeCodeTrace

A small dataset of redacted Claude Code (`claude --bare -p`) interaction traces, captured against a self-hosted Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct fp8 vLLM backend with LMCache cacheblend retrieval. Designed to support research on KV-cache reuse, prompt-cache hit-rate measurement, and the structural shape of CC's request bodies (skill prefixes, tool definitions, `/compact` summaries).

**License:** CC-BY 4.0
**Maintainer:** [@intelchen](https://huggingface.co/intelchen)
**Schema:** [`claudecode_trace_schema.md`](./claudecode_trace_schema.md)
**Source code:** [`intelc/skillcacher-public`](https://github.com/intelc/skillcacher-public) (MIT)
**Generated:** 2026-05-09

## Related publication

This dataset is the benchmark artifact for:

> **Hit Rate Is Not Output Quality: Characterizing KV-Cache Reuse on Agent Traffic.**
> Yiheng "Intel" Chen, University of Pennsylvania, 2026.
> PDF + sources: [`intelc/skillcacher-public`](https://github.com/intelc/skillcacher-public/blob/main/skillcacher-paper.pdf).

The paper uses three subsets of this dataset (n=99 main corpus, n=47 deep-evaluation subset, n=19 divergent-judged slice) to measure cacheblend rescue rates, TTFT, output token-identity, and an LLM-judge agent-protocol preference rate at $T=0$ on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct fp8.

> **Note on the HF Dataset Viewer:** this dataset is structured as a tree of per-capture directories (each containing `traces.sqlite`, `tokens/*.parquet`, `vllm.log`, etc.) rather than a single sharded parquet. The HF Dataset Viewer's auto-preview won't render rows directly; browse via the **Files and versions** tab and load individual artifacts with `huggingface_hub.snapshot_download` or `pyarrow.parquet.read_table`.

## Subsets

| Subset | Capture style | Top-level dirs | Captures |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| `swebench_verified` | `claude --bare -p` against an SWE-Bench Verified problem statement; one-shot, agentic | 5 | 5 |
| `post_compact` | Multi-turn `claude --bare -p --resume` sessions including a `/compact` turn | 7 | 7 |
| `skill_invocation` | Hand-crafted `(skill, prompt)` pairs from `test_skills/` that explicitly invoke a SKILL.md anchor; one batch dir contains all 15 (skill, prompt) captures, since the proxy's trace-store shares a directory across the warm-pod batch | 1 | 15 |

Each entry is a directory with the layout described in `claudecode_trace_schema.md`. The headline artifacts per entry are `traces.sqlite` (per-request hit metrics), `tokens/req_*.parquet` (per-request token streams with structural tags), and `vllm.log` (engine-side LMCache hit lines).

## Methodology

Every capture flows through:

```
claude --bare -p ... \
  --base-url http://127.0.0.1:4000 \
  ──── (local skillcacher proxy) ────▶
       │
       │  (a) prepends ` # # ` separators around CC structural blocks
       │      via cc_segment_parser so cacheblend sees natural chunk
       │      boundaries on first-turn traffic;
       │  (b) normalizes per-turn `cch=` and `cc_version=` fields in the
       │      x-anthropic-billing-header so chunks 0 of the same session
       │      hash identically across turns;
       │  (c) records request body, prompt token stream, response token
       │      stream, and LMCache hit metrics into traces.sqlite + parquets;
       │
       └──▶ vLLM 0.7 + LMCache 0.4.2 (cacheblend) on a 2× H100 RunPod pod
```

Three load-bearing components keep cacheblend's STORE and LOOKUP paths chunk-aligned on this stack: a chunk-aligned LOOKUP patch to LMCache 0.4.2, a CC-aware segment parser that injects cacheblend separators around CC structural blocks, and per-turn header normalization that stabilizes chunk-0 hashes across multi-turn sessions. Without these, hit rate on natural CC traffic is 0%; with them, rescue reaches 95–99% at the steady-state peak (paper §5.1).

## Redaction

All text artifacts are scrubbed by `scripts/publish_claudecode_trace.py --apply`. The redaction surface is documented in the schema doc. Briefly: deployment-side fingerprints (RunPod URLs, Tailscale identifiers, API keys, CC build hashes) are replaced with `<REDACTED_*>` markers; user-supplied prompts, model responses, and SWE-Bench problem statements (already public) are preserved bit-exact.

The pre-publish audit script's tests verify every artifact class is caught — see `tests/test_publish_audit.py` in the source repo for the round-trip proof.

## Known limitations

1. **Llama-only.** The dataset captures `claude --bare -p` against a Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct backend. Llama doesn't emit Anthropic's `cache_read_input_tokens` field, so the `cache_read_tokens` column in `traces.sqlite` is always 0 — use `engine_total_hit_tokens` (engine-side via vllm.log scrape) instead. Captures against an actual Anthropic backend would have populated `cache_read_tokens`; that's not in scope here.

# Wisp Claude Code Sessions

Raw conversation transcripts from **Claude Code** running on a single
[Omarchy](https://omarchy.org) (Arch Linux + Hyprland) workstation, operated by
the agent persona **wisp** ([github.com/crispwisp](https://github.com/crispwisp)).

These are real, unedited agent trajectories: a human (voice-driven) working with
Claude Code on systems/dev tasks, plus nested computer-use agent runs from the
[hyprbench](https://github.com/crispwisp/hyprbench) Hyprland benchmark.

## Contents

`transcripts/` mirrors Claude Code's `~/.claude/projects/` layout. Each
subdirectory is one project (working directory); each `*.jsonl` file is one
session, one JSON record per line (user/assistant messages, tool calls, tool
results, and harness metadata).

Three broad groups:

- **`-home-me/`** — the main wisp sessions: open-ended home-directory work
  (system config, agent tooling, dotfiles). The large files are long
  multi-hour sessions.
- **`-home-me-ht-hyprland-bench/`** — development of the hyprbench benchmark.
- **`-home-me-ht-hyprland-bench-results-.../`** — auto-generated transcripts
  from individual hyprbench computer-use tasks (window management, app control,
  config edits, etc.), including workflow sub-agent logs.

## Schema

Line-delimited JSON. Common fields per record: `type` (`user`/`assistant`),
`message` (Anthropic-style `{role, content[]}`), `uuid`/`parentUuid` (turn
chain), `timestamp`, `cwd`, `sessionId`, `version`, `gitBranch`. Content blocks
include `text`, `thinking`, `tool_use`, and `tool_result`. Schema varies across
Claude Code versions — treat fields as best-effort.

## Privacy / scrubbing

Before publication the transcripts were scanned and credential values
(API keys, access tokens, account passwords) were replaced with
`[REDACTED-SECRET]`. Public identifiers (the `crispwisp` handle, its public
email, public repo names) are intentionally retained. If you spot anything
sensitive that slipped through, please open a discussion on this dataset.

## Caveats

- Tool outputs may contain transient system state, file snippets, and
  command output from the host machine.
- Computer-use task transcripts reflect benchmark scaffolding, not polished
  demonstrations.
- No guarantee of correctness — these are working sessions, mistakes included.

# Fable 5 Claude Code Traces

A full, scrubbed release of Fable 5 Claude Code session traces for researchers studying real coding-agent behavior: multi-turn prompts, assistant responses, tool calls, command output, retries, and session-level workflow metadata.

This release keeps the full package intact: **18 sessions**, **9,497 JSONL events**, **0 excluded rows**, and **0 quarantine files**. The traces are preserved in the native agent-event format so they can be inspected in Hugging Face Agent Traces / Data Studio and parsed directly for custom analysis.

## Why this dataset may be useful

- Study how coding agents interleave natural-language reasoning, shell/file tools, observations, retries, and task management.
- Build or evaluate tool-use policies, trace parsers, distillation pipelines, and agent-observability tooling.
- Inspect complete session timelines rather than isolated prompt/completion pairs.
- Compare raw agent-event logs with converted training formats used by other Fable 5 trace releases.

## Dataset contents

|---|---:|
| Claude Code session files | 18 |
| JSONL events | 9,497 |
| Assistant events | 2,506 |
| User events | 1,424 |

Files at the repository root are one scrubbed session per `*.jsonl` file. Each line is one event. `manifest.json` contains per-file row counts, event counts, scrub-count summaries, and totals.

The source traces were scrubbed before publication with a deterministic recursive scrubber over JSON keys and values. Private identifiers were replaced with stable typed placeholders while preserving the research-relevant structure of the sessions.

This dataset contains redacted Claude Code session traces exported with [cc-share-hf](https://github.com/badlogic/cc-share-hf). The traces were filtered to keep only sessions that passed deterministic redaction and LLM review.

Each file in `data/` is a redacted Claude Code session in its native JSONL format (one entry per line). HuggingFace auto-converts these to Parquet with one row per session file and four columns:

The data was processed with [cc-share-hf](https://github.com/badlogic/cc-share-hf) using deterministic secret redaction plus an LLM review step. Deterministic redaction targets exact known secrets and curated credential patterns. The LLM review decides whether a session is about the OSS project, whether it is fit to share publicly, and whether any sensitive content appears to have been missed.

Embedded images may be preserved in the uploaded sessions unless the workspace was initialized with `--no-images`.

## Limitations

This dataset is best-effort redacted. Coding agent transcripts can still contain sensitive or off-topic content, especially if a session mixed OSS work with unrelated private tasks. Use with appropriate caution.

We release coding agent traces using Claude Code for

1. Opus
    1. ISL, OSL, ISL_new counts
2. GPT-oss-120B
    1. ISL, OSL, ISL_new counts and their raw texts

For Opus, only the locally saved files from the harness were used for analysis.

Coding agents take multiple turns to carry out a task from the input prompt. To analyze the token distribution, two models were selected: Anthropic's Opus and OpenAI's gpt-oss-120B. The input sequence length (ISL), output sequence length (OSL) and the uncached, new input sequence length (ISL_new) were extracted from locally saved files or a proxy used as a middleman. The setup consists of using Claude-code as the harness, SWE-Bench Pro as the dataset. For open source models, vLLM is used as the inference server and also uses SWE-Bench Verified dataset.

Each task is solved sequentially to capture the token distribution.

Using vLLM, for each turn, the uncached tokens (prefill) and the newly generated tokens (decode) will have their KV cache computed and will be stored in blocks. In the subsequent turn, the matching KV blocks will be used. Non-matching tokens will go through prefill (ISL_new tokens), and decode will generate one token at a time (OSL tokens), repeating the cycle.

The OSL is the cumulative tokens generated in decode. ISL_new is the unique tokens without prefix cache hit (tool call result + partial OSL). ISL is the total input token (previous ISL + partial OSL + tool call results). Prefix cache hit is computed as (ISL - ISL_new) / ISL. Token counts are obtained from vLLM's prometheus loggers, measured in per turn sensitivity. Opus has these metrics that are accessible in the local computer inside `~/.claude/projects/<sanitized-cwd>/<session_id>.jsonl`.

For opus, ISL, OSL and ISL_new are computed as

```
isl     = input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + cache_read_input_tokens
isl_new = isl − cache_read_input_tokens
osl     = output_tokens
prefix_cache_hits = cache_read_input_tokens
```

We define a *run* as one execution of a model configuration against a whole dataset. A run may consist of multiple sessions. A *session* is an agent's attempt on solving a single task from a prompt request to the harness. A session may consist of multiple turns. A ***turn*** is a single harness-mediated interaction step within a session. A turn is usually a single inference request.

Submitting a prompt to Claude code, it may send title-generation requests to vLLM. These are independent to the task at hand, and have ~50 shared tokens with the system prompt, altering the actual workload prefix cache metrics. These are filtered using a proxy.

# Real Pi Coding Agent Traces Sessions

An aggregated dataset of **real human–AI coding agent sessions**, collected from 21 independently published Hugging Face datasets and hand-filtered to exclude synthetic or AI-generated content.

Every session is an unedited (but redacted) trace of a real person using [pi](https://pi.dev) — an open-source AI coding agent harness — to build, debug, and ship real open-source software. Real prompts, real tool calls, real errors, real backtracking.

## Why this dataset exists

Most "agent interaction" datasets on Hugging Face are synthetic: LLM-generated prompts, simulated users, templated tasks, scripted scenarios. They're useful for some things, but they systematically lack the properties that make real agent traces valuable:

- **Real problem statements** — vague, typo-ridden, context-dependent human prompts, not cleanly specified tasks
- **Real failure and recovery** — tool errors, wrong assumptions, dead ends, backtracking, iterating on a design that didn't work
- **Real complexity** — multi-file refactors, API quirks, environment issues, type errors, dependency hell
- **Real tool-use patterns** — actual sequences of `read` / `bash` / `edit` / `write` calls against real codebases, with real outputs
- **Real reasoning** — thinking blocks from reasoning models working through genuine ambiguity

If you're doing **distillation, SFT, or trajectory-level training for coding agents**, the gap between synthetic and real data matters. This dataset is an attempt to gather the real supply that already exists, scattered across many small single-project datasets, into one place.

## Dataset at a glance

| Stat | Value |
|------|-------|
| Total sessions | 1,291 |
| Source datasets | 21 |
| Total messages / turns | 192,309 |
| Approx. tokens | ~194,000,000 |
| Date range of sessions | 2025-12-01 → 2026-06-18 |
| Format | newline-delimited JSON ([pi session format](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/session.md)) |
| Primary languages | English prompts; TypeScript, Java, Python, Lua, and more in code |

## What's in a session

Each `*.jsonl` file is one complete agent session in [pi session format](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/session.md): newline-delimited JSON containing:

| Content | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| User prompts | What the human actually asked the agent to do |
| Assistant responses | Code, explanations, analysis, plans |
| Tool calls | `read`, `bash`, `edit`, `write`, and custom extension tools — the actual operations performed |
| Tool results | Command output, file contents, compiler errors, test failures |
| Thinking blocks | Model reasoning (where reasoning models were used) |

Schematic (illustrative, abbreviated):

```json
{"type": "message", "role": "user", "content": "the websocket gateway drops connections after ~30s, figure out why"}
{"type": "message", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"type": "thinking", "thinking": "..."}, {"type": "text", "text": "Let me look at the gateway code..."}, {"type": "tool_call", "name": "read", "arguments": {"path": "src/gateway.ts"}}]}
{"type": "tool_result", "name": "read", "content": "..."}
```

Sessions span a wide range of real development work: architecture design, feature implementation, debugging, test fixing, integration work (Discord bots, WebSocket gateways, Ollama providers), tooling development, and open-ended experimentation.

# Agent trace dataset

## Decoding the literal token IDs

The `prompt_token_ids` / `completion_token_ids` / `logprobs` columns are the
verbatim tokens the serving engine emitted, stored PER AGENT STEP as a
list-of-lists (one inner list per turn). To turn them back into text you MUST
use the exact tokenizer the model was served with — a generic same-family
tokenizer will decode word tokens to garbage.

Served model / tokenizer source: `Qwen/Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-FP8`

```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
# Use the served model's own tokenizer (pull from the ref above; if it is a
# gs:// mirror, copy tokenizer.json/tokenizer_config.json/vocab.json/merges.txt
# locally first and point AutoTokenizer at that dir).
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-FP8")
# token_ids are list-of-lists (one list per turn) — decode each turn:
text = [tok.decode(turn, skip_special_tokens=False) for turn in completion_token_ids]
```

Engine-reported served model name: `1783165012733068`

See `tokenizer_provenance.json` for a machine-readable version.

# dacorvo/hf-hub-session-captures

HTTP captures of agent ↔ model interactions — one parquet row per
`/v1/chat/completions` call. Produced by
[agentcap](https://github.com/huggingface/agentcap).

Native session traces for the same runs live in companion datasets
named `hf-hub-session-<agent>-traces`. They're all grouped under the
[hf-hub-session Collection](https://huggingface.co/dacorvo)
alongside this dataset. Join on `run_id`.

## Loading

```python
from datasets import load_dataset

ds = load_dataset("dacorvo/hf-hub-session-captures", split="train")
```

## Schema

| column | description |
|---|---|
| `run_id` | agentcap run id; matches the per-run folder in the traces dataset |
| `request_id` | UUID minted by the capture proxy |
| `model` | Model id from the captured request body |
| `captured_at` | Epoch seconds when the request was captured |
| `request` | Raw OpenAI request body, JSON-stringified |
| `response` | Raw OpenAI response body, JSON-stringified (or `{"stream": true, "raw": ...}` for SSE) |
| `served_by` | Per-response `X-Served-By` header (HF Router sub-provider routing) |
| `served_build_info` | Per-response `X-Build-Info` header |
| `served_model` | Per-response body-echoed `model` |
| `provider` | Derived from the proxy upstream URL (constant per file) |
| `upstream_url` | Proxy upstream URL at capture time (constant per file) |

`request` and `response` are JSON strings; consumers `json.loads(...)`
them. To recover per-message token ranges, render `request.messages`
through the model's chat template yourself —
`transformers.AutoTokenizer.apply_chat_template`.

## Sharing traces with Swival

Swival can export full conversation traces with `--trace-dir`, which writes one `<session_id>.jsonl` file per session:

```bash

# SynthTraces

![synthtraces-banner](https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/5dd96eb166059660ed1ee413/0KEiR1V6QfFU3jzMpvqlr.png)

A minimal codebase to generate **synthetic coding agent session traces** using [Pi](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent).

Each session pairs **two models** working inside one of the project codebases:

- a **remotely hosted open model** (e.g. `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro`, `openai/gpt-oss-120b`, `Qwen/Qwen3.6-27B`) backs the **coding agent**, equipped with the default Pi tools — `read`, `write`, `edit`, and `bash`;
- a **local model** running in llama.cpp plays the **user**, opening with one of the starting questions and driving the conversation.

The full exchange is recorded as a trace. The dataset is the cartesian product of every agent model × user model × codebase × starting question.

## Generation matrix

| Dimension                            | Count      | Examples                                                                                                            |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Agent models (remotely hosted, open) | 20         | `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro`, `openai/gpt-oss-120b`, `Qwen/Qwen3.6-27B`, `zai-org/GLM-5.1`, …                      |

| Project codebases                    | 20         | `transformers`, `diffusers`, `lerobot`, `peft`, `candle`, …                                                         |
| Starting questions                   | 20         | _"How do I run this code?"_, _"How is CI set up in this repo?"_, _"What recent changes were made and why?"_, …      |

```text

                        ▼
        ┌────────────────────────────────┐
        │  USER MODEL · local, llama.cpp │   plays the user
        └───────────────┬────────────────┘

        ┌───────────────┴────────────────┐
        │  PROJECT CODEBASE  (1 of 20)   │   cloned locally
        └───────────────┬────────────────┘

# ox-alpha-pi-traces-emacs-bridge

Dataset converted from
[TeichAI/Ox-Alpha-Pi-Traces](https://huggingface.co/datasets/TeichAI/Ox-Alpha-Pi-Traces)
so every `write`, `edit`, and `read` tool call runs through a
generic MCP server (`tools`) that wraps Emacs editing via
[python-bridge](https://github.com/manateelazycat/python-bridge).

## Layout

- `ipython/` — 2246 traces rewritten as `ipython` REPL cells.
  Each cell uses `await mcp.call_tool("tools", "ox-bridge-write", {...})` etc.,
  with the discovery call (`await mcp.list_tools("tools")`) inserted
  before the first bridge call.
- `tools/` — 2246 traces with named tool calls (`ox-bridge-write`,
  `ox-bridge-edit`, `ox-bridge-read`) and a `bridge_source` field
  containing the equivalent ipython cell.
- `final_v1/` — deterministic curation snapshot (freeze
  `afe9aef614d24268245c7970f68eac5dfac1dd9296d606cf82d06ffb83703266`).
  Contains `manifest.json`, `schema.json`, `quality_report.json`,
  curation labels, explicit-only goal review, negative-example candidates,
  lexical leakage review, reviewed queue decisions, splits, and
  `checksums.sha256`.
- `system_prompt.md` — the prime-agent ACP system prompt,
  extended with a section explaining the `tools` MCP server.
- `tool_schema.json` — JSON Schema of every tool exposed by the
  `tools` MCP server.
- `convert_traces.py` — converter used to regenerate both trace folders.
- `ox_trace_bridge.el` — Emacs Lisp bridge implementation
  (`ox-bridge-write`, `ox-bridge-edit`, `ox-bridge-read`).

## Curation snapshot (final_v1)

Covers 2,246 traces: 2,212 valid and 34 quarantined.

- **Outcomes**: 2,118 success, 39 partial_success, 17 inconclusive, 38 failure, 34 quarantined
- **Difficulty**: 792 easy, 1,197 medium, 257 hard
- **Negative examples**: 339
- **Leakage groups**: 311 (0 cross-split groups)
- **Splits**: train 1,521 / review 280 / test 228 / validation 175 / quarantine 42

The snapshot is reproducible, but semantic labels remain evidence-based
candidates: the manifest and quality report keep
`human_approval_required: true`. Raw traces are never modified by
finalization. The expected-negative heuristic (tests/assertions built to
demonstrate failure are not task failures) is applied in
`finalize_dataset.py::classify_outcome` (295 traces flagged
`expected_negative_demo=true`).

Verify integrity with:

```bash
cd final_v1 && sha256sum -c checksums.sha256
```

## Bridge channel

Every editing operation goes through the `tools` MCP server.
For example, a write cell looks like:

```python
result = await mcp.call_tool("tools", "ox-bridge-write", {"path": "x.py", "content": "# ...\n"})
print(result)
```

Before the first editing call of each trace, the model sees a discovery
cell:

```python
tools_list = await mcp.list_tools("tools")
for t in tools_list:
    print(t["name"], t["inputSchema"])
```

This matches the prime-agent runtime contract: `mcp` is pre-imported,
`mcp.list_tools(server)` returns the live tool schema, and
`mcp.call_tool(server, name, args)` invokes the tool. There are no
`import` statements in any generated cell — the runtime guarantees that
the `mcp` object is already in scope.

## Emacs side

To run the `tools` MCP server backed by Emacs:

1. Start Emacs and load `ox_trace_bridge.el`:
   ```
   (add-to-list 'load-path "/path/to/python-bridge")
   (require 'python-bridge)
   (python-bridge-enable)
   (load-file "/path/to/ox_trace_bridge.el")
   ```
2. Run `mcp_bridge/server.py` with the prime-agent MCP stdio harness,
   or wire it as a generic MCP server.

## Regeneration

```bash
python convert_traces.py traces/ ipython/ --system-prompt system_prompt.md
python convert_traces.py traces/ tools/  --system-prompt system_prompt.md --mode tools
python finalize_dataset.py --root dataset_build --output dataset_build/final_v1
```

`convert_traces.py` expects `traces/*.jsonl` in the original pi/teich
format (one JSON object per line, `type: message` with `role: assistant`
and `content: [{type: toolCall, ...}]`).

# Coding agent session traces for thomasmustier/pi-for-excel-sessions

This dataset contains redacted coding agent session traces exported with [pi-share-hf](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-share-hf) from a local [pi](https://pi.dev) workspace. The traces were filtered to keep only sessions that passed deterministic redaction and LLM review.

## Data description

Each `*.jsonl` file is a redacted pi session. Sessions are stored as JSON Lines files where each line is a structured session entry. Entries include session headers, user and assistant messages, tool results, model changes, thinking level changes, compaction summaries, branch summaries, and custom extension data.

Pi session files are tree-structured via `id` and `parentId`, so a single session file may contain multiple branches of work. See the upstream session format documentation for the exact schema:

- https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/session-format.md

Source git repo: https://github.com/tmustier/pi-for-excel

## Redaction and review

The data was processed with [pi-share-hf](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-share-hf) using deterministic secret redaction plus an LLM review step. Deterministic redaction targets exact known secrets and curated credential patterns. The LLM review decides whether a session is about the OSS project, whether it is fit to share publicly, and whether any sensitive content appears to have been missed.

Embedded images may be preserved in the uploaded sessions unless the workspace was initialized with `--no-images`.

## Limitations

This dataset is best-effort redacted. Coding agent transcripts can still contain sensitive or off-topic content, especially if a session mixed OSS work with unrelated private tasks. Use with appropriate caution.

# Agent Manager session — designing session sharing

> **Access: public.** Anyone with the link can read this trace. Public is the only mode
> where the Hub's trace viewer works for every visitor regardless of account tier.

A single real [Agent Manager](https://huggingface.co/spaces/lvwerra/agent-manager-template)
session, exported as a shareable trace. This is the working session in which the
session-sharing design itself was researched and written — surveying how five coding-agent
harnesses persist sessions, testing what the Hub's trace viewer can do, and producing a
design doc.

## View it

Open **Data Studio** and click the single row: the Hub renders the full session — prompts,
assistant turns, tool calls, token counts, thinking blocks. The repo holds one session, so
it is always `row=0`, which makes it directly embeddable:

```html
<iframe src="https://huggingface.co/datasets/thomwolf/am-session-sharing-design/embed/viewer/default/train?row=0"
        frameborder="0" width="100%" height="700px"></iframe>
```

## What's in here

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
|  `<session-uuid>.jsonl` | the session, verbatim Claude Code JSONL (a Hub-native trace format) |
| `meta/manifest.json` | provenance: harness + version, session ids, stats, content hash, lineage |
| `meta/briefing.md` | mechanically generated handoff summary — what was asked, tools used, files written |
| `meta/redaction.json` | which redaction rules ran and what they caught |

## Session at a glance

- **Harness**: Claude Code 3.3a · `claude-opus-5[1m]`
- **7** user prompts · **38** assistant turns · **40** tool calls
- **95,795** input / **39,337** output tokens (2.68M cache read)
- Tools: `Bash` ×23, `Read` ×6, `WebSearch` ×4, `WebFetch` ×4, `Skill`, `ToolSearch`, `Write`

## Provenance and redaction

Exported by the phase-1 prototype described in the design doc: locate → redact → assemble
→ publish. Before upload the trace went through redaction ruleset v1 — token-shaped
patterns (`hf_`, `sk-ant-`, `gh?_`, AWS, Google, JWT, private keys), **value** matching
against the Space's actual secret-bearing environment variables, and an email rule.

Result: **no secret matches**, 7 email addresses redacted (shown as `«redacted:email»`),
and 8 `file-history-snapshot`/`delta` lines dropped — those embed full file contents and
are the single worst leak vector in a Claude transcript.

The source code visible in this trace belongs to Agent Manager, which is published as a
[public template Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/lvwerra/agent-manager-template);
the files quoted here were verified byte-identical to that public copy before publishing.

Traces can still contain local paths, command output and private context. Review before
publishing your own.

## Forking it

The transcript filename is a Claude Code session id, so a recipient can continue this
conversation: place  `<session-uuid>.jsonl` at `<CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR>/projects/<cwd-slug>/<new-uuid>.jsonl`
and run `claude --resume <new-uuid>`. Always **copy** — `--resume` appends to the
transcript, so resuming a shared artifact in place would mutate the thing that was meant
to be frozen. `meta/manifest.json` records `trace.nativePath` for exactly this.
